exercises.prompt: In the `Temperatures` unit, why is the constant `Freezing` declared in the implementation section rather than the interface?

options.label: Because only the unit's own code needs it; declarations in the implementation are invisible to other units and programs
options.feedback: Yes. Keeping it private means it can change without affecting any user of the unit.

options.label: Because constants are not allowed in an interface section
options.feedback: Not yet: interfaces may declare constants, types, variables and routines.

options.label: Because the implementation section is compiled first
options.feedback: Not yet: the order of compilation is not the reason. Visibility is.

hints: What happened when a program tried to use Freezing?
exercises.solution: Anything declared only in the implementation section is **private to the unit**. A program that uses `Freezing` gets `Identifier not found`. Put in the interface only what users need, so everything else can change freely.

exercises.prompt: A program using the `Temperatures` unit calls `Describe(30)`, then `Describe(0)`, then `ToFahrenheit(10)`, and prints `ConversionCount`. What number is printed?

feedback.message: Not yet: look at Describe's test. Is 0 <= Freezing?

hints: Describe converts only when the temperature is above Freezing.
Freezing is 0.0, and the test is C <= Freezing.
exercises.solution: `Describe(30)` converts (1). `Describe(0)` takes the freezing branch, because 0 <= 0, and does not convert. `ToFahrenheit(10)` converts (2). The program printed `Conversions: 2`.

feedback.message: Not yet: P points at X itself, so P^ := … changes X.

hints: `@X` is the address of X, and `P^` is the value at that address.
exercises.solution: `P` holds the address of `X`, so `P^` *is* `X`. Multiplying `P^` by 3 changes `X` to **15**.

exercises.prompt: Using the lesson's `Push` and `Pop`, starting from `Top := nil`, a program does: `Push(Top, 'a'); Push(Top, 'b'); Push(Top, 'c'); Pop(Top); Pop(Top); Push(Top, 'd');` and then prints the values from the top down, separated by spaces. What does it print?

feedback.message: Not yet: the stack is printed from the top, and d was pushed last.
Not yet: the two pops removed c and b.

hints: Pop removes the most recently pushed value.
exercises.solution: After three pushes the stack is c, b, a (top first). Two pops remove c and b, leaving a. Pushing d puts it on top: **d a**.

exercises.prompt: In the tree program, the word list is replaced by the same words in alphabetical order: `banana, date, kiwi, kiwi, kiwi, lime, mango, mango, papaya, yam`. What depth does the program report now?

feedback.message: Not yet: the shape of a search tree depends on the order of insertion, not just on the set of words.
Not yet: repeated words are counted in an existing node, not inserted again.

hints: Each new word is greater than all earlier ones, so where does it go?
How many distinct words are there?
exercises.solution: Each new distinct word is larger than every word already in the tree, so it always goes to the right: the tree degenerates into a list of the **7** distinct words, depth 7. This is why balanced trees (or hash tables) are used in practice.

exercises.prompt: After `P := Q; Dispose(Q); Q := nil;`, what is true of `P`?

options.label: P still holds the old address, which no longer belongs to the program's data: it is a dangling pointer
options.feedback: Yes. Using P^ now is a serious bug that may corrupt memory silently.

options.label: P is nil too, because it pointed to the same memory
options.feedback: Not yet: Q := nil changes only Q. P is a separate variable holding a copy of the address.

options.label: P still points to a valid Integer, because Dispose only marks memory
options.feedback: Not yet: after Dispose the memory may be reused for anything. Reading or writing it is undefined.

exercises.solution: `Dispose` returned the memory, and `Q := nil` protected only `Q`. `P` still holds the old address: a **dangling pointer**. Using it may read garbage or overwrite unrelated data. Track ownership so that exactly one place frees each block, and nil every pointer to it.

exercises.prompt: In the tree program, `FreeTree(Root);` is replaced by `Root := nil;`. What does the last line print, and why?

options.label: `Heap back where it started: FALSE`, because the nodes were never disposed, only forgotten
options.feedback: Yes. The seven nodes are leaked.

options.label: `Heap back where it started: TRUE`, because setting the root to nil frees the tree
options.feedback: Not yet: assigning nil frees nothing. Only Dispose returns memory allocated with New.

options.label: The program crashes
options.feedback: Not yet: leaking memory does not crash a short program. That is what makes leaks easy to miss.

hints: Does assigning nil to a pointer call Dispose?
exercises.solution: Setting `Root` to `nil` only forgets where the tree is. The nodes stay allocated, the heap in use stays larger than at the start, and the program printed **`Heap back where it started: FALSE`**: a memory leak.
